A B S T R A C T

With the extensive application of fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles, accurate fault diagnosis becomes crucial for flight safety and system reliability. Traditional fault diagnosis methods often require large datasets that are difficult to obtain in practice. To address this, we start with the spatio-temporal correlation characteristics and multi-dimensional heterogeneity of UAV flight data, and propose a multi-scale feature fusion with temporal dynamic graph network (MFFTD) that enables efficient fault diagnosis using limited UAV flight data. In the spatial dimension, a multi-scale residual convolutional design captures feature representations at various levels. Furthermore, the global temporal dynamic graph models the topological dependencies between the feature representations. In addition, we introduce long short-term memory networks to capture long-term dependencies in the temporal dimension. For cross-domain joint learning in both the temporal and spatial dimensions, we propose a multi-head feature fusion module based on mutual information to address the issue of heterogeneity imbalance between feature representations. Experiments on four public datasets demonstrated that MFFTD improves the detection accuracy by eight percentage points compared to the latest models under the 90 small-sample settings of multi-class tasks and significantly enhances the generalization capability, offering superior decision support for UAV fault diagnosis. The code and data will be available at https://github.com/17992/MFFTD.
1. Introduction

With the rapid development of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV), they are increasingly used in a wide range of fields, including military reconnaissance $[1]$ , industrial surveillance $[2]$ , agricultural spraying $[3]$ , and logistics and transport $[4]$ . The wide application of UAVs has significantly improved the work efficiency of these industries; however, it has also put forward high requirements for the safety of UAVs. Since UAVs performing tasks in complex environments $[5]$ can be affected by the external environment, hardware failures, and software defects, continuous and stable flight operation are crucial. The UAV flight process generates a large amount of highly spatio-temporally correlated and multidimensional heterogeneous data, such as flight speed, altitude, attitude, temperature, and battery power, which can provide strong support for system health. Therefore, the utilization of flight data for fault diagnosis has become a key research direction for UAV applications. Currently, techniques used for UAV fault diagnosis can be divided into two categories: model- and data-driven fault diagnosis methods.

Model-based approaches employ mathematical and physical models to analyze flight data, thereby identifying anomalies and faults. For example, Telford and Galloway [6] proposed a UAV electrical power system fault classification and diagnostic system based on hidden Markov models to assist and improve UAV health management and control. However, this method is only applicable to the binary classification of fault diagnosis tasks. In [7], a quadrotor was modeled as a linear parameter varying (LPV) system, and designed an LPV observer for fault detection; however, the LPV model was applied only to nonlinear systems within a narrow scope and was insufficient to capture complex dynamic characteristics. Another study [8] presented a mathematical model for a quadrotor UAV and proposed a robust nonlinear controller that combined the sliding-mode control and backstepping control techniques, which achieved good diagnostic results in simulation experiments. However, this method relies heavily on an accurate mathematical model of the UAV and has a poor generalization ability. In [9], actuator fault diagnosis for multirotor UAVs was proposed based on the cascade of a nonlinear Thau observer and a linearized Kalman filter. However, this method depends on the accurate linearization of the system, and complex nonlinearities impair the diagnostic performance [10] proposed an extended Kalman filter (EKF)-based fault observer for hexacopter UAV fault diagnosis and isolation and validated the effectiveness of the method on simulation data. However, the EKF is sensitive to noise and modeling errors and is prone to stability reduction by error ampli fication in practice $[11]$ proposed an actuator fault detection and diagnosis method based on EKF and multi-model adaptive estimation. However, this method incurs high development and maintenance costs and has limited versatility. Model-based approaches require accurate system modeling, have high development and maintenance costs, and vary from one UAV to another; thus, these approaches face many challenges in practical applications.

Data-driven methods, which are adaptable to learning features from data for fault diagnosis, have gained considerable attention in recent years. In $[12]$ , real flight data on a small fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle (FW-UAV) with an open-source Paparazzi autopilot system were presented, and support vector machine (SVM) algorithm was used for fault diagnosis. However, it encountered an overfitting problem. In $[13]$ signal preprocessing and feature extraction on sound data obtained from electric motors was performed using a decision tree, SVM, and k-nearest neighbors for fault diagnosis. However, it relies on manual feature engineering, making it difficult to capture the complex patterns and multiscale characteristics of fault signals, thereby limiting the diagnostic accuracy. Reference $[14]$ used graph attention networks (GAT) for fault diagnosis by treating flight data as graph structures. However, it has a low efficiency in high-dimensional graph feature learning and requires a large amount of labeled data for network training. In $[15]$ , a novel UAV fault diagnosis approach based on self-supervised contrast learning and spatial-temporal information of multivariate flight data was proposed; however, it requires large amounts of data and is sensitive to hyperparameters. The above methods relied heavily on the quality and quantity of the data and had limited performance on high-dimensional time series data. To address the scarcity of UAV failure data $[16]$ extracted temporal and spatial features from flight data by employing tandem convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and long short-term memory networks (LSTM), aiming to solve the problem of troubleshooting FW-UAVs with few-shot learning. In $[17]$ , the heterogeneous deep multitask learning (HDMTL) framework with adaptive sharing and knowledge complementation was used to explore fault diagnosis under small samples. Research $[18]$ focused on small sample multi-task fault diagnosis, enhancing model performance through multi-task joint training and proposing a novel scheme for reliable diagnosis of complex UAV systems. These models consider the problem of scarce and expensive UAV failure data; however, they are too coarse to acquire the temporal and spatial characteristics of flight data, and there is considerable scope for enhancement.

To address the above challenges, we propose fault diagnosis model Multi-Scale Feature Fusion with Temporal Dynamic graph network (MFFTD) for FW-UAV fault diagnosis. At the spatial feature extraction level, we designed a multi-scale residual convolutional module for capturing spatial information, and to capture spatial topological information, we introduced a global temporal dynamic graph to enhance the above convolution process. For timing-feature capture, we used LSTM to model the long-term dependence between timings. For feature fusion, we designed a multi-head mutual information self-attentive feature fusion module to address the data imbalance problem between spatial and temporal features, along with an advanced feature abstraction fusion process. Overall, our main contributions can be summarized as follows:

1. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to introduce global temporal dynamic graphs into small-sample drone fault diagnosis, capturing long-term spatial topological dependencies among anomalous data. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional methods in capturing the spatio-temporal characteristics of flight data.

2. To address data scarcity and imbalance, we design a multi-head mutual information self-attention feature fusion method. Through the combination of multi-head self-attention and mutual information constraints, the accuracy and robustness of anomaly detection are enhanced.

3. In designing the spatio-temporal feature extraction backbone, we incorporate a multi-scale residual convolutional method. By deeply integrating multi-scale feature extraction with residual learning, we achieve comprehensive capture and efficient representation of complex spatial features in flight data.

4. We conduct extensive evaluations on four publicly available real-world fixed-wing drone flight datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that MFFTD achieves performance across multiple metrics in fault diagnosis accuracy.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 briefly introduces the existing related research. Section 3 presents the MFFTD framework and implementation process. In Section 4, we describe the dataset, data processing, experimental analysis, ablation experiments, and visual analysis. Section 5 summarizes this study.
2. Related works

In this section, we briefly review UAV fault diagnosis, multiscale residual convolutional networks, relevant advances in temporal dynamic graphs, and attention mechanism methods for UAV fault diagnosis.
2.1. UAV Fault diagnosis

Fault diagnosis of UAV flight data is crucial for ensuring flight safety with the aim of accurately identifying potential faults by analyzing multi-dimensional time-series data $[19]$ (such as those from sensors, control commands, and environmental parameters) during the flight process. Current research mainly relies on deep-learning models for feature extraction and fault classification $[20]$ , and these methods usually achieve relatively high accuracy when there is a large amount of labeled data. However, in practical applications, owing to the complex operating environments of UAVs and limitations in data collection, an insufficient number of samples often restricts the performance and generalization ability of the models. In addition, UAV flight data exhibit significant spatio-temporal dependence characteristics, including local dynamic changes and global long-term correlations. Nevertheless, most existing methods adopt a single feature extraction mechanism $[21]$ , making it difficult to model multi-scale features simultaneously, which leads to insufficient representation of local details or a lack of ability to capture global trends. Few-shot learning has the advantage of efficiently mining deep features and reducing the cost of data collection for UAV flight failures. It is a research direction with both academic value and practical significance and can effectively solve problems such as data scarcity, label imbalance, and insufficient generalization ability.
2.2. Multi-scale residual convolutional network

Since the advent of CNN $[22]$ , significant progress has been made in their application to drone fault diagnosis research. We adopt a tabular review approach $[23]$ for organization and summarization as shown in Table 1.

However, traditional CNNs have limitations in feature extraction such as a fixed receptive field, poor adaptability to scale variations, and the vanishing gradient problem, which hinder their ability to capture complex patterns. In the context of fault diagnosis for UAV flight data, CNNs struggle to balance global and local feature extraction, thereby constraining diagnostic performance. We have previously introduced a multi-scale residual convolutional network (MRCN) $[28]$ in the field of UAV fault diagnosis for the first time. By integrating convolutional kernels of varying sizes, MRCN effectively expands the receptive field, enabling the simultaneous capture of global trends and local details within the data. This capability is particularly advantageous for handling scale-variant characteristics inherent in fault signals. Furthermore, the incorporation of residual connections $[29]$ mitigates the vanishing gradient problem, thereby improving training efficiency and feature representation in deep architectures. These advantages underscore the potential of MRCN as a highly effective approach for UAV fault diagnosis, demonstrating exceptional applicability in this domain.

text: 2.3. Global temporal dynamic graphs

Graph neural networks (GNN) have been demonstrated to effectively capture complex dependencies in temporal data, showcasing powerful capabilities in feature extraction and relationship modeling. In recent years, GNNs have attracted increasing attention in the field of flight fault data diagnostics. CLGNN $[30]$ leverages GNNs to model sensor signals represented in a graph structure. A temporal dynamic graph (GTDG) is a graph network design capable of effectively addressing the variability of temporal data and dynamic nature of graph structures. GTDG has achieved significant success in multidimensional temporal data analysis $[31]$ . TD-Graph-LSTM $[32]$ was proposed to address action-driven, weakly supervised object detection by propagating the temporal context over a per-frame dynamic graph structure, which can alleviate the problem of missing labels per frame. In the field of multivariate time-series classification, TodyNet $[33]$ was designed as an end-to-end temporal graph neural network to capture dynamic time-series features adequately through dynamic graphs. However, during temporal dynamic graph fusion, TodyNet suffers from error accumulation and cannot handle missing or unequal-length data. CATodyNet $[34]$ was proposed to address these issues. However, the aforementioned methods focused on designing temporal dynamic graphs from a local perspective of long-term dependencies, making it challenging to directly model flight fault data with limited samples. Consequently, the application of temporal dynamic graphs from a global perspective in the domain of small-sample flight fault diagnostics requires further investigation.
2.4. Attention-based methods for UAV fault diagnosis

Owing to the successful application of attention-based transformer architectures in natural language processing $[35]$ , an increasing number of attention mechanisms are being incorporated into UAV fault diagnosis. The most recent results are presented in Table 2.

However, these methods overlook the imbalance between spatiotemporal features and the accumulation of information errors during fusion. In this study, we proposed an MHMIFF module. It employs a multi-head mechanism to compute spatiotemporal mutual information independently, and encodes multidimensional feature correlations to retain discriminative information while eliminating redundancy. During the fusion, a linear layer with normalization and dropout prevents dimensional explosions and suppresses ineffective features, thereby enabling efficient and compact feature fusion.

text: 3.1. Problem formulations

FW-UAV flight data record the vehicle's flight status with strong spatiotemporal correlations and multidimensional heterogeneity. Assume that is a dataset available for training $F = \{ (X_i, Y_i) \}_{i=1}^S$ , where $X_i$ and $Y_i$ are the samples and their labels, respectively, and $S$ is the number of samples. The sample $X = \{ x_t \}_1^T$ is a sequence of lengths T, where each time step $x_t$ is an $F$ -dimensional vector. Formally, $x_t = [x_t^1, x_t^2, \ldots, x_t^F]$ , where $x_t^F$ is the value of the $F$ th feature at time $t$ . Specifically, the vector form of the sample is $X \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times F}$ . The fault sample $X_i \neq f(z)$ , where $f(z)$ represents the normal operation mode of the aircraft and $z$ denotes the operational input of the aircraft. In the fault diagnosis process, the spatial features $In_{spa}$ and temporal features $In_{tem}$ are captured by the MRCN, GTDG, and LSTM networks, respectively, and then undergo feature fusion through the MHMIFF.

3.3. GTDG

Influenced by CATodyNet $[34]$ , we enhanced the capture of spatial topological relationships by introducing GTDG into the backbone. In contrast, we define the dynamic graph using an initialization approach, where the adjacency matrix is fully populated with ones, representing a complete graph structure at the beginning. In the context of few-shot learning for fault diagnosis, a dynamic graph does not exhibit partition cutting properties. 3.5. MHMIFF

However, this parallel design lacks effective prior knowledge and strategies for guiding the integrated learning process. Simple feature fusion methods such as concatenation or weighted summation of outputs from two dimensions may introduce redundant information. However, these methods lack the ability to abstract high-level features and potentially suffer from the curse of dimensionality. To address these issues, we propose the MHMIFF. In the MFFTD architecture, MHMIFF serves as the core module for deep spatiotemporal feature fusion, addressing key challenges such as redundancy and dimensional explosion. Unlike simple concatenation-based fusion methods, MHMIFF leverages a mutual information encoding mechanism to construct bidirectional cross-domain dependencies between spatial and temporal features. By quantifying shared information using Eq. (19), the model dynamically attends to informative regions while filtering out irrelevant content, effectively reducing redundancy at the source. Furthermore, the multi-head self-attention mechanism decomposes feature processing into multiple subspaces, where each head independently computes attention over the transformed features $M_{i}^{q}$ , $M_{i}^{k}$ , and $M_{i}^{v}$ , enabling the parallel abstraction of high-level representations while maintaining a controlled output dimensionality. Additional refinement through linear transformation and layer normalization ensures the efficient integration of features. These mechanisms enhance the model's ability to learn complex spatiotemporal patterns, thereby improving both diagnostic accuracy and generalizability.
3.6. Loss function

The following will elaborate in detail on the design logic, components of the loss function in MFFTD, and its impact on the optimization process.

In fault classification tasks, cross-entropy loss (CE) is a commonly employed metric for measuring the discrepancy between the model's predicted probability distribution and the ground-truth label distribution. 3.7. Time-complexity analysis

In this section, we analyze the time complexity of MFFTD based on the data flow illustrated in Algorithm 1. Given an input multivariate time-series tensor $X \in R^{B \times T \times F}$ , where B is the batch size, T is the time sequence length, and F is the number of input features, we break down the time complexity of each major module of MFFTD as follows:

The model initialization and fault label assignment steps are independent of the input size and are thus considered constant in time complexity: $\mathcal{O}(1)$ . The time-windowing operation sampleProduction constructs historical sequences from raw data, resulting in complexity linear in the time dimension and window length: $\mathcal{O}(T \cdot F \cdot n_{\mathrm{step}})$ .

Each MultiScaleConv block processes input features using multiple 1D convolution kernels of different sizes. For input $X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times F \times T}$ and kernel size $k$ , each convolution operation has a time complexity of: $\mathcal{O}(B \cdot F \cdot T \cdot k)$ . Assuming $K$ total kernel sizes per layer, the total complexity per convolution block becomes: $\mathcal{O}(B \cdot F \cdot T \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{K} k_i)$ .

Each LSTM layer processes sequences of shape $(B,T,F)$ with hidden size $H$ . The time complexity per LSTM layer is approximately: $\mathcal{O}(B\cdot T\cdot H^2)$ . Since three LSTM layers are applied sequentially, the total complexity for the temporal module is: $\mathcal{O}(3\cdot B\cdot T\cdot H^2)$ .

MHMIFF modules perform cross-modal attention between convolutional and LSTM features. Each MHMIFF contains two MultiHeadAttention layers. Given input sequence length T, feature dimension F, and h heads, the attention complexity per head is: $\mathcal{O}(T^{2} \cdot F/h)$ . Thus, the total complexity per MHMIFF module becomes: $\mathcal{O}(2 \cdot B \cdot T^{2} \cdot F)$ . This is the dominant term in MFFTD due to the quadratic dependence on T, the sequence length. Three MHMIFF modules contribute: $\mathcal{O}(B \cdot T^{2} \cdot F)$ .

A learnable adjacency matrix $A \in R^{T \times T}$ is applied multiple times to propagate correlations across variables. Matrix multiplication has a time complexity of: $\mathcal{O}(B \cdot T^{2} \cdot F)$ . However, due to the fixed size T, this term is typically small relative to attention and convolution operations.

The final fully connected layers map feature vectors of size D to output logits. Given layer width F, the complexity is: $\mathcal{O}(B \cdot F^{2})$ . Since this module is applied twice (once for spatial, once for temporal), the combined cost is: $\mathcal{O}(2 \cdot B \cdot F^{2})$ .

Summing the dominant components, the overall time complexity per iteration is approximated as: $\mathcal{O}(B\cdot T^{2}\cdot D+B\cdot T\cdot H^{2}+B\cdot F\cdot T\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{K}k_{i}+B\cdot T\cdot F^{2})$ . Here, the quadratic term $\mathcal{O}(B\cdot T^{2}\cdot F)$ from the MHMIFF module dominates when T is large, due to the self-attention mechanism over time sequences. Hence, MFFTD scales efficiently with moderate input lengths but can incur higher cost with very long sequences.

4.2. Methods for comparison

In this section, we review the relevant literature and select state-of-the-art and classical methods based on traditional machine learning or neural networks to comprehensively evaluate the performance of MFFTD. The benchmarks used are summarized below.

1. SVM [12]: SVM is a classical machine learning algorithm where the goal is to find a hyperplane that completely separates the different classes of data points and maximizes the distance of the two classes of data points to this hyperplane.
2. CANN [44]: CANN is an attention-based convolutional neural network model with multiple spatial and channel attention modules.

3. SHNN [16]: SHNN is a few-shot learning approach to address FW-UAV fault diagnosis by employing multiple series-connected CNN and LSTM networks to capture the spatio-temporal features of flight data.

Simultaneously, the dependencies between some nodes are attenuated, with the emergence of blue areas in tandem. In Fig. 12(e) and (f), the weight distribution begins to become more concentrated. The red and blue areas are more conspicuous, and their values are lower. These alterations signify that the spatial topological relationships have been thoroughly learned and reinforced by the model, further corroborating that the model is capable of capturing more transitive topological relationships within a global context.

To verify the effectiveness of MHMIFF, we visualized its interior of MHMIFF using the model that was trained with 90 samples on the dataset of July 21st, as shown in Fig. 13. Fig. 13(a) presents the weight distribution of the multi-head attention mechanism after training in the MHMIFF module. The attention mechanism measures the importance of the input features. The higher the weight, the brighter the color, indicating a more significant relationship. In the initial training stage, the heatmap showed a uniform color, indicating that the model treated all features equally without capturing the feature relationships, and there was no significant interaction among the features. As the training progressed, the weight range expanded and the heatmap appeared in a strip shape, with the intensity of the feature interaction increasing and the weights of some features increasing. In the final stage, the heatmap becomes highly sparse and the weight range expands further, demonstrating that the model has clearly identified the most crucial features for the task, thus validating the effectiveness of the attention mechanism in feature selection.

text: 4.9. Feasibility analysis

In practical engineering, the collection of flight data from FW-UAVs is susceptible to environmental factors such as electromagnetic interference and aerodynamic vibration, which results in the data of the sensors being superimposed with random noise, severely restricting the stability of fault diagnosis models. The experimental results show that the accuracy of all models decreases with decreasing SNR (i.e., increased noise). Furthermore, models trained on the July 23rd dataset demonstrate better stability, as the higher wind speed on that day led to more noise in the collected data compared to the July 21st dataset, enabling more adequate training and thus stronger stability. In conclusion, the experiments fully validate that the unique design of MFFTD endows it with superior noise-resistant robustness and engineering applicability in practical engineering scenarios characterized by scarce fault data and existing noise interference.

Moreover, in practical applications, the parameter scale and single-sample inference time of MFFTD are compatible with common UAV embedded hardware; meanwhile, its sensor integration has simple requirements, only needing a 50Hz sampling frequency and configuration of 12 types of UAV flight attitude sensors. Thus, this technology exhibits favorable practical feasibility in real-world scenarios.

text: 5. Conclusion

To address the scarcity of flight fault data, this study differs from conventional data augmentation or few-shot learning methods and focuses on the spatiotemporal correlation characteristics and multidimensional heterogeneity of UAV flight data. Based on small samples, we proposed MFFTD. We designed a multi-scale residual convolutional network to comprehensively capture the spatial features of flight data, introduced a global temporal dynamic graph to achieve topology enhancement, and utilized an LSTM network to mine the temporal features deeply. In addition, a novel multi-head mutual information self-attention feature fusion module was designed to dynamically weigh the spatiotemporal features, addressing the issue of feature fusion imbalance. Under the conditions of limited flight data, the fault diagnosis accuracy of MFFTD significantly surpasses that of the previous models. However, the model's multi-component architecture introduces high complexity and a large parameter count, limiting its deployment in resource-constrained UAV systems; meanwhile, practical deployment must contend with complex environmental disturbances like temperature fluctuations, electromagnetic interference, and sensor noise. Future research should thus focus on simplifying the structure to reduce computational costs without compromising accuracy, while further exploring robustness under such varying operating conditions. Furthermore, MFFTD has been experimentally verified to exhibit stability in the generalization dimensions of cross-time-series, cross-scenario, and cross-distribution features, laying a foundation for its extended applications. Meanwhile, it can be further extended to potential generalization directions, including cross-equipment models, cross-workloads, and cross-environmental interferences, incorporating the fault diagnosis needs of other UAVs or multimodal flight data, and integrating with advanced technologies to enhance robustness and real-time performance, to better meet the needs of UAV safe flight missions.
